newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton backs binding targets on greenhouse gases.
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs binding targets on greenhouse gases.

text.p: President Bill Clinton plans on Thursday to commit Washington to "significant" cuts in greenhouse gases and pledge $1 billion of U.S. aid to help developing nations reduce their emissions, officials said.
But the United States will reject European Union targets for sharp cuts in the gases that cause global warming as "impossible," the officials said.

In a speech to the U.N. Earth Summit on Thursday night Clinton intended to recognise that the United States, the world's biggest polluter, has "clear responsibilities" to control its emissions of carbon dioxide, they said.
For the most part the $1 billion aid plan would involve money already earmarked for foreign assistance.

In a briefing before Clinton's speech to the summit, the officials said he would pledge specific limits on emissions at an international conference on global warming in Kyoto, Japan at the end of the year.

Katie McGinty, head of the administration's Council on Environmental Quality, read from a passage in Clinton's prepared remarks in which he will pledge to "bring to the Kyoto conference in December a strong American commitment to realistic and binding limits that will significantly reduce our emissions of greenhouse gases."
Greenhouse gases that cause climate-changing global warming were one of the most contentious issues at last weekend's summit of industrialised nations in Denver.
European leaders there slammed Clinton for refusing to accept strict targets for cutting greenhouse emissions.
The G7 communique said the rich nations' club wanted clear and realistic targets for cuts but avoided the European Union target of a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010.

"The president states clearly and unequivocally that the science is clear and compelling on this, states clearly and unequivocally that the United States will take this issue on ... that we are going to work in Kyoto for a legally binding agreement that will significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions," McGinty said.
Asked about the targets sought by the EU, McGinty said, "It is impossible to achieve 15 to 20 percent reductions in that time period."

She said that "for the United States, those numbers are not realistic" and stressed the administration's attitude toward reducing emissions was that "We want to do this with the kind of seriousness of purpose that says we know that we will get there."

The Earth Summit began earlier this week with U.S. allies, like British Prime Minister Tony Blair and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, chiding Clinton for failing to show resolve in dealing with global warming.
The United States accounts for 23 percent of greenhouse gas emissions and environmentalists say all efforts to combat the problem are doomed without strong U.S. action.

Clinton would also announce in his speech that he will host a White House conference in the fall to discuss global warming and generate broad public support for eliminating greenhouse gas emissions, the officials said.
In his speech he also was to announce a programme to install one million solar units on the rooftops of homes and businesses throughout the United States by the year 2010.
The federal cost for the project would be about $200 million annually, acording to administration officials.
